newsitem.title: USA: Senate opposes more U.S. military base closures.
newsitem.headline: Senate opposes more U.S. military base closures.

text.p: The Senate voted by a two-to-one margin on Wednesday to block until the year 2001 additional military base closings sought by the Defense Department.

The 66-33 vote, which crossed party lines, was on an amendment to the $268 billion defense spending bill, which the Senate hopes to complete work on this week. The amendment would allow already authorized base closures to go ahead.
The House already passed its version of the defense bill, omitting the authorization of base closings.

Defense Secretary William Cohen, backed by the Joint Chiefs of Staff, had wanted two more rounds of domestic base closures in 1999 and 2001, partly to help pay for billions of dollars in high-tech weaponry for the 21st century.
Cohen estimated the next two rounds would save about $2.7 billion a year.

But the Senate voted to delay the next round until early in the 21st century, pending further analysis by the Pentagon and government economists of how much the closures actually save. That review would have to be completed early enough to allow Congress to consider more closings in the year 2001.

The vote also reflected Republican anger over what they perceived as politically motivated meddling by President Clinton before the 1996 election with what was supposed to be a streamlined, nonpolitical procedure. He stopped closures at two Air Force maintenance facilities that employed thousands of civilians in vote-rich California and Texas.
"We're going to close bases on military merit, not electoral votes," Oklahoma Republican Sen. Don Nickles said, explaining why he backed postponing more closures.
The amendment was sponsored by Sen. Byron Dorgan, a North Dakota Democrat, and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican.
It does not stop or slow down nearly 100 bases targeted for shut-downs and 55 for realignment under earlier rounds of closures.
Shutting down bases is a politically painful process, as nearby communities are often heavily dependent on the military facilities for jobs and commerce.
Dorgan said nearly one-fourth of domestic and foreign bases had been targeted for closure since the end of the Cold War with uncertain economic benefits.
"Let us not authorize (closures) until we figure out the consequences," he said.
But opponents, who also crossed party lines, said refusing to cut military facilities was in effect taking money away from the troops.
Sen. John McCain, an Arizona Republican who had spearheaded the drive to authorize more closures, said it would be "Orwellian" logic to argue that shutting down a base would not save money.
"It's the strangest argument I've ever heard in my years in the Senate," said McCain, a former prisoner of war in Vietnam. "We will continue to siphon off money that our troops need."
The earlier closures were done under a streamlined Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) procedure, but that system had expired and a new one had to be authorized.
